structure.title: Cover -  Notice of AGM and Annual Report
structure.summary: This letter to stock exchanges announces Bharti Airtel's 30th AGM on August 8, 2025, via video conferencing, and the distribution of the Notice and Integrated Annual Report for FY 2024-25. The Notice and report are sent by email to members with registered email addresses as of July 11, 2025, and physically to others with access links and QR codes. It details e-voting facilities (remote and at AGM), the cut-off date (August 1, 2025), and remote e-voting period (August 4-7, 2025). The documents are enclosed and available on the company website. The letter includes company contact information, regulatory compliance references, and signature, with annexures listing the annual report, AGM notice, and physical communication. The attached report cover page is also included.

structure.title: Annual Report
structure.summary: The Annual Report covers Bharti Airtel’s FY 2024-25 performance, strategy, governance, financials, and ESG. It details business segments (Mobile, Broadband, DTH, IPTV, Airtel Business, Passive Infrastructure), 5G/AI investments, customer metrics, and financial highlights. It includes Chairman/MD messages, Board and committee details, corporate governance, risk management, stakeholder engagement, materiality, and value creation model. The report presents standalone and consolidated financial statements with auditor’s reports, notes on accounting policies, related party transactions, leases, and risk management. It covers ESG commitments, sustainability initiatives, CSR, Bharti Airtel Foundation, awards, and regulatory compliance. Additionally, it contains the AGM notice, explanatory statements for resolutions, and disclosures on cost auditors, secretarial auditors, and related party transactions, along with shareholder information and corporate office details.

nodes.title: Annual Report (intro)
nodes.summary: This Integrated Report and Annual Financial Statements 2024-25 for Bharti Airtel Limited covers the company's customer-obsessed approach and safe network, detailing integrated services (Mobile, Broadband, DTH, IPTV, digital/financial services, enterprise connectivity, data centers), investments in 5G and AI-powered networks, and AI-driven anti-spam solutions. It presents FY 2024-25 financial highlights (consolidated and standalone revenue, EBITDAaL, net profit), customer metrics (India, Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka), ESG ratings, and recognition. The report includes an overview, performance, strategy, board messages, value creation, stakeholder engagement, materiality, ESG approach, risk framework, KPIs, CSR, awards, and featured stories on mobile, homes, experience, network, spam protection, ESG, financial, B2B, and digital. It outlines reporting period, boundary, principles, assurance, contents, and cautionary statements.

nodes.summary: The text outlines Airtel's strategy built on strategic pillars: acquiring and retaining quality customers with differentiated services, micromarketing via a unified customer view, accelerating digital through an integrated platform, and delivering brilliant experiences from search to referral. nodes.title: FROM COMMITMENT
nodes.summary: The text outlines Airtel's commitment to ESG principles integrated across operations to build a sustainable and inclusive future. It highlights rural connectivity expansion to over 85 million people, enabling education, healthcare, commerce, and digital banking. Environmental efforts include reducing carbon footprint via 'Green 5G' with Nokia using AI/ML, solarizing network sites, and deploying lithium-ion and VRLA batteries. Diversity and inclusion initiatives are emphasized, with women comprising over 60% of campus recruits and 18.5% of the workforce. Strong governance, integrity, transparency, and enhanced disclosures like EBITDAaL are noted, along with leadership succession planning. Key metrics include over 30K solar-powered sites in two years, over 64% network sites tagged 'Green', and over 2 million liters monthly diesel reduction. CRISIL GVC Level-1 grading sustained for nearly two decades is also mentioned.

nodes.title: Connecting Responsibly for Limitless Impact
nodes.summary: Airtel outlines its sustainability strategy, emphasizing scientific evidence and key priorities like climate action, circular economy, gender equality, digital inclusion, and waste management. The vision is to be a globally renowned ESG-led company through leading practices and transparent reporting. The text also details Airtel's sustainability journey from 2018 to 2025, highlighting milestones such as publishing its first Integrated Report, becoming the first telecom company with validated SBTi targets, developing an ESG governance structure, and publishing the first SEBI-BRSR. It lists numerous awards and recognitions, including Golden Peacock Awards, CDP ratings, MSCI rating, and DJSI membership, showcasing continuous progress in ESG performance and reporting.

nodes.title: Staying Ahead in an Unpredictable Landscape
nodes.summary: The section covers Airtel's risk management framework amid volatile markets, detailing responsibilities across the Board, Risk Management Committee, and operational teams, and outlining a process from environmental scanning to governance reporting. It lists ten top risks: regulatory/political uncertainty, economic uncertainty, network/IT quality, competition, internal control gaps, data loss prevention, cost structures, network experience amid data growth, lack of digitization/innovation, and climate change. Each risk is elaborated with context, impact, and mitigation strategies, including stakeholder engagement, hedging, network redundancy, AI/ML personalization, compliance automation, DLP, cost optimization, 5G rollout, digital-first strategy, and climate-proofing infrastructure. The section also highlights customer experience initiatives like omnichannel platforms, AI-powered anti-spam, and self-care tools, with metrics on spam reduction and service efficiency.

nodes.title: Airtel Risk Management: Responsibilities, Process, and Top Risks
nodes.summary: The page outlines Airtel's risk management approach amid volatile Asia and Africa markets, citing political, economic, regulatory, technological, competitive, climate, and data privacy risks. It details responsibilities across the Board, Risk Management Committee, Chief Risk Officer, management, and operational teams for risk oversight and mitigation. The risk identification and management process includes environmental scanning, classification, measurement, accountability assignment, action plan development, prioritization, resource allocation, performance monitoring, and governance reporting. Finally, it lists ten top risks: regulatory/political uncertainty, economic uncertainty, network/IT quality, competition, internal control gaps, data loss prevention, cost structures impacting liquidity, network experience amid data growth, lack of digitization/innovation, and climate change/energy management.

nodes.title: Regulatory and Political Uncertainties (Legal and Compliance)
nodes.summary: The text covers three risk categories for Airtel: regulatory and political uncertainties, economic uncertainties, and network/IT quality, plus a competitive battleground section. For regulatory/political risks, it discusses operating in politically unstable regions, impacts like spectrum pricing and verification norms, and mitigation through stakeholder engagement, neutral government relations, CSR, industry bodies, and compliance oversight. Economic uncertainties involve currency fluctuations, inflation, and supply chain disruptions, mitigated by diversification, hedging, local currency contracts, debt diversification, supply chain resilience, and mark-to-market pricing. Network/IT risks include technical failures and disasters, mitigated by network operations centers, in-house planning, redundancy, infrastructure sharing, automation, and disaster recovery plans. Competitive pressures in 5G and broadband are addressed via AI/ML personalization, omni-channel, spam protection, unlimited 5G, FWA, IPTV, and differentiated content.

nodes.title: Bharti Airtel Risk and Mitigation Framework: Economic Uncertainties and Network/IT Risks
key_items: Poor Quality of Networks and IT, including Redundancies and Disaster Recoveries (Operational)
nodes.summary: The page presents Bharti Airtel's risk and mitigation framework for two operational risks. Economic Uncertainties: context of emerging markets with low penetration and income, challenges from capital controls, inflation, interest rate volatility, currency fluctuations, and import dependence; impact on consumer spending, foreign currency borrowings, and supply chain disruptions; mitigating actions include diversification across services and markets, prudent cash management with hedging and local currency conversion, debt diversification, derivative instruments, supply chain strategy with digital systems and indigenous manufacturers, and mark-to-market pricing. Poor Quality of Networks and IT: context of technical failures, partner failures, human errors, natural disasters, equipment delays, software errors, fiber cuts, lack of redundancy, weak disaster recovery, erratic IT connectivity, and poor IT staff quality; impact on network and IT systems; mitigating actions include infrastructure sharing, state-of-the-art Network Operations Centres, in-house network planning, quality improvement programs, redundancies, performance measurement, disaster management guidelines, Network Recovery Plans, removal of single points of failure, MPLS network, climate proofing, and automated operations.

nodes.title: Fiercely Competitive Battleground (Operational)
nodes.summary: The text outlines five operational and strategic risks for Bharti Airtel: fierce competition, internal control gaps, data loss prevention, rising costs ahead of revenues, and inability to provide high-quality network experience amid data growth. Each risk includes context, impact, and mitigating actions. Competition focuses on cross-selling, AI/ML personalization, 5G, and fixed wireless access. Internal controls emphasize compliance, automation, audits, and financial reporting. Data loss prevention covers privacy regulations, DLP software, and monitoring. Cost pressures are addressed via the War on Waste program, capex optimization, digitization, and debt management. Network experience mitigation includes capacity investments and seamless service to retain customers.

nodes.title: Airtel Risk and Mitigation Framework: Operational and Strategic Risks
key_items: Gaps in Internal Controls (Financial and Non-financial) (Operational)
Gaps in prevention of Data Loss (Operational)
Increase in Cost Structures ahead of Revenues thereby Impacting Liquidity (Operational/Strategic)
nodes.summary: The page outlines Bharti Airtel's risk and mitigation framework for three key risks: gaps in internal controls (financial and non-financial operational), gaps in prevention of data loss (operational), and increase in cost structures ahead of revenues impacting liquidity (operational/strategic). Each risk section includes outlook from last year (stable), capitals impacted, material issues, context, impact, and mitigating actions. Internal controls risk covers governance, compliance, and financial reporting, with mitigations like IT investments, audits, and compliance tools. Data loss risk addresses data privacy regulations (GDPR, DPDP Act) and mitigations including DLP strategies, endpoint/web/email protection, and monitoring. Cost structure risk discusses rising costs and mitigations like the War on Waste program, capex optimization, digitization, and debt management.

nodes.title: Inability to Provide High-quality Network Experience with Exponential Growth in Data Demand (Strategic)
nodes.summary: The text addresses the strategic risk of failing to provide high-quality network experience amid exponential data demand growth, citing stable outlook from last year and material issues like product innovation and customer experience. It explains the impact of rising data demand and competition, then details Airtel's multi-pronged mitigation strategy: network densification with small cells, Massive MIMO, and new macro sites; backhaul upgrades including 45k Rkm fiber rollout; broadband expansion with 7.2 million FTTH home passes; spectrum acquisition of 54.8 MHz across 12 circles and refarming in seven circles; 5G rollout with ~130,000 BTS serving 135 million+ users; large-scale network expansion and modernization deploying over 20K sites, including rural areas, and upgrading 4G/5G capabilities; Fixed Wireless Access scaling to over 1 million connections; and AI/ML models for traffic prediction, energy efficiency, and cell optimization, alongside customer tools like Thanks App and QoS dashboards.

nodes.title: Lack of Digitisation and Innovations (Strategic)
nodes.summary: The text addresses the strategic issue of lack of digitisation and innovation for Airtel, noting its emerging outlook from last year and impact on material issues like digital inclusion and ICT access. It outlines the telecom sector's rapid digital transformation, evolving customer expectations for digital content, apps, mobile financial services, AI, edge solutions, SaaS, and sovereignty needs. It explains the impact: internal processes must adopt digital transformation quickly or Airtel risks falling behind changing customer preferences. Mitigating actions include a digital-first approach, talent capability, and a three-pillar digital strategy: new digital-first products, simplified customer lifecycle via self-service and omni-channel, and a digital core for experience and efficiency. It also cites the Integrated Report and Annual Financial Statements 2024-25.

nodes.title: Climate Change and Energy Management (Strategic)
key_items: Flood-prone areas design criteria; Water-scarce areas design criteria; Cyclone and wind-prone areas design criteria
Cyclone and wind-prone areas design criteria
nodes.summary: This text from Bharti Airtel's 2024-25 Integrated Report addresses climate change and energy management as a strategic outlook. It identifies material issues including climate change, energy efficiency, emission reduction, and sustainable supply chain management. Airtel assessed physical and transition risks, noting that natural disasters degrade telecom infrastructure, disrupt services, raise costs, hinder repairs, and pose safety risks. Mitigating actions involve climate-proofing infrastructure with specific design criteria for flood-prone areas (elevated foundations, flood-resistant materials, early warning systems), water-scarce areas (rainwater harvesting, recycling, leak detection), cyclone/wind-prone areas (safety factors, permanent structures, proper equipment installation, maintenance), and temperature-related risks (reflective roofs, green roofs, shading, heat-resistant materials).

nodes.title: EXCEPTIONAL EXPERIENCES ACROSS
nodes.summary: Airtel outlines its customer obsession strategy built on platform-led simplicity and network excellence. It covers the omnichannel 'Buy, Bill, Pay, Serve' platforms for intuitive customer journeys, now scaled to B2B, and digital-first engagement with self-care, real-time issue resolution, and personalized offers. Advanced digital tools provide 100m x 100m network visibility for proactive management and precision interventions. An AI-powered Anti-SPAM solution, an industry first, has flagged billions of unwanted calls and SMS, improving transparency and trust. Metrics show 26.2 billion SPAM calls and 1.4 billion+ SPAM SMS notified, notifications in 10 Indian languages, and reductions of over 17% in B2C interactions and over 18% in service requests in two years.

It also provides consolidated financials (shareholders' equity, net debt, capital employed) and key ratios such as capex productivity, opex productivity, EBITDA margin, EBIT margin, return on shareholders' equity, return on capital employed, net debt to EBITDA, interest coverage ratio, book value per equity share, net debt to shareholders' equity, and earnings per share (basic). nodes.title: Empowering Minds, Transforming Communities
nodes.summary: The section covers Bharti Airtel Foundation's education initiatives, including the Satya Bharti School Program operating 164 rural schools with holistic development and community involvement, and the Quality Support Program in government schools across 12 states with various clubs and digital literacy. It highlights higher education partnerships and scholarships, and shares inspiring alumni stories like Rajnish Sharma, Rajendra Lal Sain, and Lovepreet Bawa, demonstrating the transformative impact of education. The Foundation reports significant reach and impact since 2000, with detailed metrics for FY 2024-25, and emphasizes equitable access, girl child education, and alignment with NEP 2020.

nodes.title: Education
nodes.summary: Bharti Airtel Foundation, the philanthropic arm of Bharti Enterprises, has provided quality education to underprivileged rural children in India since 2000, focusing on equitable access for girls, school-level programmes, and higher education partnerships aligned with NEP 2020. It reports impact since inception (3.7 million students, 36,000+ schools, 3.3 million community members, 3.3 lakh+ teachers) and during FY 2024-25 (22 lakh+ students, 16,000+ schools, 1.9 lakh+ teachers). Airtel supports the Foundation through Satya Bharti Schools, a Quality Support Program in government schools across 12 states, employee volunteering, a two-week placement for Young Leaders, and mentoring TheTeacherApp.

nodes.title: Satya Bharti School Program
key_items: Enabling Savings for Rural Households; CASE STUDY
nodes.summary: The Satya Bharti School Program, launched in 2006 by the Bharti Airtel Foundation, operates 164 rural schools across four Indian states, serving over 37,000 students. It provides free, quality education with a focus on holistic development and the girl child, offering books, uniforms, shoes, and mid-day meals. The program integrates digital tools, project-based learning, innovative teaching, and co-curricular activities. It recruits local teachers and supports their professional development through training. Community involvement and volunteer participation are encouraged to enhance school operations and student growth. The initiative has helped rural families save approximately ₹400 crores, with support expanded in FY 2024-25 to include free shoes, socks, and school bags, based on NSS data and inflation adjustments.

nodes.title: Beyond Boundaries: Journey from Satya Bharti School to Airtel
nodes.summary: The section highlights Rajnish Sharma's transformative journey from a Satya Bharti School student to an Airtel wireman, alongside Monika's testimonial on teaching her grandmother through Saksharta Bharti Abhiyan. It details the Quality Support Program (QSP) launched in 2012-13, covering 12 states, 1,000 schools, and 4 lakh+ students (51% girls), built on four pillars: inspired leadership, empowered students, involved parents/community, and enhanced school environment. Key initiatives include life skills clubs, internships (300+ schools, 200+ institutes, 9,300+ students), IT Innovation Clubs (450+ clubs, 5,200+ students, 700+ projects), Astronomy Clubs (400+ schools), Digital Literacy (10,000+ students), State Partnerships (15,000+ schools, 17 lakh+ students), and TheTeacherApp (118,000+ users, ~300 learning hours). Higher education partnerships with institutions like Plaksha University, IIT Delhi, IIT Bombay, ISB Mohali, J.C. Bose University, University of Cambridge, and Anant National University, plus the Bharti Airtel Scholarship for engineering students (276 recipients, 22% girls in 2024-25). Case studies of alumni Rajendra Lal Sain (AIIMS Jodhpur) and Lovepreet Bawa (Indian Army) are presented. Performance metrics are as of March 2025, part of the Integrated Report and Annual Financial Statements 2024-25.

nodes.title: Quality Support Program (QSP)
nodes.summary: This text highlights Rajnish Sharma's journey from a Satya Bharti School student to an Airtel wireman, emphasizing education's transformative power. It includes a testimonial from Monika about teaching her grandmother via Saksharta Bharti Abhiyan, and details the Quality Support Program (QSP) launched in 2012-13 to transform government schools. QSP's reach is noted (12 states, 1,000 schools, 4 lakh+ students, 51% girls), along with its four foundational pillars: inspired leadership, empowered students, involved parents/community, and enhanced school environment. Key initiatives described are life skills clubs, internships (300+ schools, 200+ institutes, 9,300+ students), and IT Innovation Clubs (450+ clubs, 5,200+ students, 700+ projects).

nodes.title: Bharti Airtel CSR: Quality School Programme Pillars and Initiatives
key_items: Key Initiatives under QSP Building life skills
nodes.summary: The page outlines Bharti Airtel's CSR programme, built on four foundational pillars: inspired school leadership and teachers (engaging teachers as change-makers), empowered students (building confident, goal-setting lifelong learners), involved parents and community (strengthening schools through active participation), and an enhanced school environment (vibrant spaces fostering creativity and collaboration). It details key initiatives under the Quality School Programme: building life skills through clubs and houses systems in Government schools, with activity-led modules to develop leadership and confidence; and internships aligned with NEP 2020, offering structured 1–10 day placements in local banks, LIC offices, universities, post offices, food processing units, and Digital Seva Kendras to build pre-vocational and employability skills. Impact figures as of March 2025 show 300+ schools, 200+ partner institutes, and 9,300+ students completing internships. The page is part of the Integrated Report and Annual Financial Statements 2024-25.

nodes.title: IT Innovation Clubs
nodes.summary: The text covers IT Innovation Clubs in government schools, which build STEM skills through coding, design, and hardware projects using starter kits and mentors; Astronomy Clubs that provide telescope access and sky-viewing, extending to neighboring schools; Digital Literacy under the Quality Support Program, teaching basic IT tools and cyber safety with student Digital Explorers; Quality Support Program State Partnerships scaling NEP-aligned interventions via teacher training and district-level support; and TheTeacherApp, a platform offering high-quality content to empower teachers and school leaders. Impact statistics as of March 2025 are provided for each initiative.

nodes.title: Empowering Change: Journey from Satya Bharti School to medical success
nodes.summary:
Empowering Change: Journey from Satya Bharti School to medical success
Rajendra Lal Sain, an alumnus of Satya Bharti School in Belwa Ranaji, is a true testament to the power of determination and education. Born into a modest family, with his father, Shivlal Sain, working as a barber and his mother, Jatudevi, as a homemaker, Rajendra excelled academically from a young age. After completing his early education at Satya Bharti School, Rajendra’s father encouraged him to pursue higher studies despite financial constraints. Determined to succeed, Rajendra moved to Jodhpur, where he rented a small room and juggled his medical studies with a night job as an ATM security guard from 2017 to 2019.

nodes.title: Breaking Barriers: Journey from a small village to joining the Indian Army
nodes.summary: The text describes Lovepreet Bawa from Panwan Village, Punjab, who attended Satya Bharti School from 2010 with parental support. He excelled academically and in sports like races and Kabaddi, scoring 97.5% in Grade 5. He continued at Satya Bharti Adarsh Senior Secondary School, Jhaneri, maintaining excellence in CBSE exams and becoming a village role model. In October 2023, he joined the Indian Army. The text also covers Rajendra, who, during medical training, was inspired to help rural villagers with high medical costs. He secured a temporary technician position at AIIMS Jodhpur in April 2020, earned a permanent role in 2022 with a monthly salary of ₹60,000, helped alumni secure positions at AIIMS, and inspires students by sharing his journey, emphasizing education and perseverance. The document includes sections labeled Overview and Performance, and CSR by Bharti Airtel Limited.

nodes.title: A. Telecommunications Act, 2023

It details the Department of Telecommunications' public consultation process for framing rules and lists six notified rules from August to December 2024, covering Digital Bharat Nidhi administration, Right of Way, telecom cyber security, critical infrastructure, temporary service suspension, and lawful interception. It also mentions process changes for Right of Way permission, including a 90% refund if denied and a 15-day timeline for bank guarantee return.

nodes.title: B. Telecommunications (Administration of Digital Bharat Nidhi) Rules, 2024 dated August 30, 2024
nodes.summary: The Telecommunications (Administration of Digital Bharat Nidhi) Rules, 2024 replace the Universal Service Obligation Fund with the Digital Bharat Nidhi (DBN), preserving existing arrangements until expiry. Right of Way permissions are time-bound, with final approval within 67 days or deemed approved. The DBN Administrator formulates implementer selection procedures, enters agreements, disburses funds, and monitors work. Rules cover temporary networks, private property networks, common ducts, cable corridors, network removal/relocation, and damage. No RoW cost increase from 2016 Rules; submarine cables included in fee schedule and pit compensation only for horizontal drilling. Implementers are selected via bidding for telecom services in underserved areas or via applications for R&D. Funding forms include full, partial, co-funding, risk mitigation, and risk capital. Funding targets underserved groups like women, persons with disabilities, and weaker sections. Scheme criteria include service provision, network creation, next-gen technologies, affordability, innovation, R&D, indigenous technology, start-ups, and standards development. The Right of Way Rules, 2024, effective January 1, 2025, are mandatory for states, with central government stakeholder engagement. Composite billing is implemented in 11 states, and the Green Energy Open Access policy notified in 24 states.

nodes.title: D. Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security)
nodes.summary: The text covers four sets of Indian telecom rules from 2024. The Telecom Cyber Security Rules mandate open sharing of DBN networks, apply to all telecom entities, allow government access to traffic data, and impose obligations like appointing a security officer, adopting a cyber security policy, reporting incidents within six hours, conducting audits, and setting up Security Operations Centres. They also grant government powers to suspend or disconnect telecom identifiers, maintain a repository, and prohibit services. IMEI registration is required. The Right of Way Rules amend definitions for mobile towers and include submarine cables. The Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure Rules require entities to provide network details for CTI notification and comply with specifications, with a review committee to examine suspension orders within five days. Digital implementation via a government portal is also covered.

New amendments adopted during the year
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (‘MCA’), vide notification no. G.S.R. 492(E) dated August 12, 2024, issued the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, 2024, introducing a new accounting standard, Ind AS 117 relating to the accounting of Insurance Contracts and MCA through notification no. G.S.R. 554(E) dated September 9, 2024, issued the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Second Amendment Rules, 2024, amending Ind AS 116 relating to the accounting for sale and leaseback transactions with variable lease payments. It identifies the ultimate controlling entity (Bharti Enterprises), entities with control (Bharti Telecom) and significant influence (Pastel Limited, Singapore Telecommunications). It lists associates, joint ventures (Indian and foreign), and other related parties with whom transactions occurred, including fellow companies and entities where key management personnel exercise influence. nodes.title: Related Parties: Associates, Joint Ventures, and Other Entities
nodes.summary: The page lists related parties under Notes to Standalone Financial Statements, all amounts in Indian Rupees millions. It covers Associates (Indian and Foreign), Joint Ventures (Indian and Foreign), and Other entities (Fellow Companies/Subsidiaries). Indian associates include Airtel Payments Bank, Oneweb India Communications (w.e.f. September 21, 2024), Hughes Communications India and its subsidiaries, Lavelle Networks, and Dixon Electro Appliances. Other entities include fellow subsidiaries Bharti Enterprises and Bharti Management Services.

nodes.title: b. Associates
nodes.summary: This section of Bharti Airtel's 2024-25 standalone financial statements covers related party disclosures, including lists of associates, other related parties, and key management personnel, with transaction summaries and arm's length statements. It details related party transactions and balances (sales/purchases, loans, guarantees, dividends, etc.), KMP remuneration, and SEBI-required loan disclosures. Lease disclosures under Ind AS 116 cover right-of-use assets, lease liabilities, and lessor accounting. Financial risk management is detailed: foreign currency risk (exposures, derivatives, sensitivity), interest rate risk (sensitivity), price risk (investments), credit risk (receivables, ECL, ageing), and liquidity risk (maturity profiles, reconciliations). Capital risk management includes net gearing ratio. Fair value disclosures categorize financial assets/liabilities with valuation methods. Title deeds not in company name and a disputed Punjab license fee matter are described. Financial ratios are presented with variances and explanations. Struck-off companies with outstanding balances are listed, and fund flow, audit trail, and scheme compliance disclosures are provided.

nodes.title: b. Associates (intro)

It lists associates (Bharti AXA Life Insurance), other related parties (e.g., Bharti Holdings, Del Monte Foods, Dixon Electro Appliances) with effective dates, and key management personnel including executive and non-executive directors with appointment/cessation dates. It states transactions are at arm's length and provides a summary table of transactions with subsidiaries, joint ventures, associates, entities with significant influence, and other related parties for March 31, 2025 and 2024, covering items like sale/purchase of assets, services, loans, guarantees, dividends, and donations. It also details significant related party transactions for sale/purchase of fixed assets/bandwidth, rendering/receiving of services with specific entities and amounts.

nodes.title: 35Leases
nodes.summary: This note covers leases: as lessee, a reconciliation of right-of-use assets by class (bandwidth, plant and equipment, building, land, laptop) for FY2025 and FY2024; descriptions of each asset class; amounts recognized in profit and loss (interest on lease liabilities, short-term and low-value lease expenses) and cash flows (principal payments); maturity analysis of lease payments; lease liability split between current and non-current. As lessor, it covers operating leases including IRU arrangements, rental income, maturity analysis of lease receivables, and a statement that gross carrying amount and depreciation of leased assets cannot be computed. It also introduces financial and capital risk management, detailing governance and foreign currency risk.

nodes.title: Lease Disclosures and Financial Risk Management Overview
nodes.summary: The page presents Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statement notes on leases under Ind AS 116, detailing amounts recognized in profit and loss (interest on lease liabilities, short-term and low-value lease expenses), cash flow principal payments, and maturity analysis of lease liabilities (current and non-current). It also covers lessor accounting for operating leases, including IRU arrangements, rental income, and maturity analysis of lease receipts, noting inability to disclose gross carrying amount and depreciation. Finally, it introduces financial risk management, listing market risks (foreign exchange, interest rate, price), credit risk, and liquidity risk, along with governance by senior management and the Board, and a policy against speculative transactions.

nodes.title: i. Foreign currency risk
nodes.summary: The text covers financial risk management disclosures: foreign currency risk, including exposure from monetary assets/liabilities and forecast transactions, risk management policy using derivatives, foreign currency exposure tables for March 31, 2025 and 2024, and sensitivity analysis showing profit/loss and equity impacts for ±5% exchange rate changes. It also details interest rate risk from floating-rate borrowings, management via swaps and fixed/floating mix, and sensitivity of profit before tax to ±100 basis point changes for 2025 and 2024. Price risk from investments in mutual funds, debt funds, government securities, and fixed deposits is discussed, noting diversification and minimal risk for short-term instruments. Credit risk is addressed, focusing on trade receivables, bank deposits, debt securities, mutual funds, and derivatives, with trade receivables noted as widely distributed and non-interest bearing, and creditworthiness assessed by management.

nodes.title: Bharti Airtel Foreign Currency Exposure and Sensitivity Analysis
nodes.summary: This page from Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statements covers foreign currency exposure and sensitivity. It presents tables showing exposure in Indian Rupees to US Dollar and EURO for trade receivables, borrowings, equipment supply payables, trade payables, net assets/liabilities, derivative assets, forward and option contracts, and net exposure as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It also includes a foreign currency sensitivity analysis table detailing the impact of a ±5% change in exchange rates for US Dollars and Others on profit/(loss) before tax and equity (OCI) for both years. The text explains that sensitivity is mainly due to USD-denominated borrowings, derivatives, and trade payables/receivables, based on reasonably possible rate changes assuming other variables constant, and that management considers these rates reasonable benchmarks.

nodes.title: iv.
nodes.summary: The text covers interest rate risk, including its definition, exposure from floating-rate debt, management via debt mix and swaps, and sensitivity analysis showing profit impact from basis point changes for 2025 and 2024 in INR and USD. It also addresses price risk from surplus fund investments in mutual funds, debt funds, government securities, and fixed deposits, mitigated by diversification, with short-tenure instruments posing minimal risk. Credit risk is defined, covering trade receivables with no concentration due to diverse customers, creditworthiness reviews, payment terms of 14-30 days (7-90 for Airtel business), ECL provision matrix, impairment thresholds of 90/120 days past due, and ageing analysis. Finally, it covers credit risk management for financial instruments and cash deposits through board-approved policies, high-credit-rated counterparties, and ongoing creditworthiness reviews.

nodes.title: (v) Liquidity risk
nodes.summary: The text covers liquidity risk management, including monitoring liquidity positions, maintaining financing sources, and assessing future cash needs. It presents maturity profiles of financial liabilities and derivatives as of March 31, 2025 and 2024, and reconciles liabilities from financing activities, detailing non-cash transactions. It also discusses capital risk management, focusing on maintaining a stable capital structure and net gearing ratio, and discloses the fair value of financial assets and liabilities by category and level, including valuation methods and key inputs.

nodes.title: Non-Cash Transactions Disclosure and Capital Risk Management
nodes.summary: The page covers two sections from Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statements. Section vii discloses non-cash transactions for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024, including right-of-use asset additions via leases, allotment of equity shares against FCCB conversions, conversion of unsecured loans into equity and debentures, and transfers of equity investments and IOT business against debentures. Section 2 details capital risk management objectives: safeguarding going concern, supporting growth, ensuring covenant compliance, and maintaining optimal capital structure. It explains monitoring via net gearing ratio and presents comparative figures for net debt, equity, total capital, and net gearing ratio as of March 31, 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: 37Fair value of financial assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: This text covers fair value disclosures of financial assets and liabilities by category (FVTPL, FVTOCI, amortised cost) with carrying and fair values, valuation methods and key inputs, and no transfers between fair value levels. It also details title deeds of immovable properties not held in the Company's name, including property descriptions, gross carrying values, title deed holders, reasons, and related merger schemes. Additionally, it describes a disputed Punjab license fee matter from 1996–1998 with ongoing litigation, and presents various financial ratios (current, debt-equity, debt service coverage, return on equity, trade receivables turnover, net capital turnover, net profit, return on capital employed, return on investment) with numerators, denominators, comparative figures, variances, and explanations for significant changes.

nodes.title: Title Deeds Not in Company Name and Other Matters
key_items: 38Title deeds of immovable properties not held in name of the Company

Section 38 details immovable properties (land, buildings, right-of-use assets) whose title deeds are not held in the Company's name as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It lists the relevant line items, gross carrying amounts, title deed holders (Amrit Bottlers Pvt. nodes.title: 40Ratios
nodes.summary: The text presents financial ratio calculations for Bharti Airtel Limited, showing numerators and denominators for ratios such as current, debt-equity, debt service coverage, return on equity, trade receivables turnover, net capital turnover, net profit, return on capital employed, and return on investment, with values for March 31, 2025 and 2024 and variance percentages, plus explanations for variances over 25%. It also includes notes to standalone financial statements listing numerous struck-off companies with outstanding balances categorized by transaction nature (payable/receivable) and balance size, along with the relationship and names of those companies.

nodes.title: 41 Nature of transaction
nodes.summary: This text from Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statements covers: a list of struck-off companies with outstanding balances (categorized by amount and nature of transaction as payable/receivable) as of March 31, 2024 and 2025; a disclosure that no funds were advanced/loaned/invested by the Company to intermediaries for ultimate beneficiaries during FY2025, with details of such transactions in FY2024 involving Bharti Airtel Services Limited and Airtel Limited as intermediaries investing in Beetel Teletech Limited and Nxtra Data Limited; and statements on audit trail implementation across IT applications (enabled in phases, effective, no tampering, data retained for 8 years) and compliance with approved schemes of arrangements.

nodes.title: Notes on fund flows, audit trail, and scheme compliance
nodes.summary: The page covers three sections from Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statements. Section 42 details that no funds were advanced or received with intermediary understanding in FY2025, and provides specifics of FY2024 transactions where funds were given to two wholly-owned subsidiaries (Bharti Airtel Services and Airtel Limited) which then invested in ultimate beneficiaries (Beetel Teletech and Nxtra Data), including amounts, dates, and relationships. Section 43 discusses the audit trail: assessment of IT applications, phased enablement, full coverage by year-end, effective operation, no tampering, and 8-year data retention. Section 44 states that all approved schemes of arrangements have been accounted for in accordance with the schemes and accounting standards.

nodes.title: 43 Audit trail
nodes.summary: The text covers notes to Bharti Airtel's standalone financial statements: Note 42 details that no funds were advanced or received with intermediary arrangements in FY2025, but in FY2024 funds were given to two wholly-owned subsidiaries (Bharti Airtel Services Ltd and Airtel Ltd) which invested in ultimate beneficiaries (Beetel Teletech Ltd and Nxtra Data Ltd), including dates, amounts, registered addresses, CINs, relationships, and acquisition details. Note 43 describes the audit trail implementation across IT applications, phased enablement, effectiveness, no tampering, and 8-year data retention. Note 44 states compliance with approved schemes of arrangements, accounted per the Scheme and accounting standards.

nodes.title: 44 Compliance with approved schemes of arrangements

First, for the year ended March 31, 2025, it states no funds were advanced, loaned, or invested by the Company to intermediaries for ultimate beneficiaries, nor were funds received from funding parties for similar purposes. Second, for the prior year ended March 31, 2024, it details funds given to two wholly-owned subsidiaries (Bharti Airtel Services and Airtel Limited) as intermediaries, which then invested in ultimate beneficiaries Beetel Teletech Limited and Nxtra Data Limited, including dates, amounts, registered addresses, CINs, relationships, and a note on share acquisition. Third, it discusses audit trail implementation across IT applications, noting phased enablement, effectiveness, no tampering, and an 8-year data retention period. Finally, it confirms all approved schemes of arrangements were accounted for in accordance with the Scheme and accounting standards.

It outlines the basis for opinion, key audit matters (revenue recognition, mobile money restricted cash, provisions for tax and regulatory matters, and accounting for acquisition of controlling stake in Indus Towers), and the auditor’s responses. It also covers information other than the financial statements, management’s responsibilities, auditor’s responsibilities, other matter regarding an associate audited by another auditor, and the report on other legal and regulatory requirements, including CARO reporting and audit trail requirements.

nodes.title: Annexure “A” to the Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: This annexure to the Independent Auditor's Report covers the audit of internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements of Bharti Airtel Limited and its Indian subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures as of March 31, 2025. It outlines management's and the Board's responsibilities for establishing and maintaining these controls based on the ICAI Guidance Note, and the auditor's responsibility to express an opinion based on audit procedures. It defines internal financial controls, acknowledges their inherent limitations, and provides the auditor's opinion that the controls were adequate and operating effectively. It also includes an Other Matter paragraph noting reliance on another auditor's report for an associate company and the auditor's signature.

nodes.title: Consolidated Balance Sheet
nodes.summary: The text presents the Consolidated Balance Sheet of Bharti Airtel Limited as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, in millions of Indian Rupees. It details assets (non-current and current) including property, plant and equipment, capital work-in-progress, right-of-use assets, goodwill, other intangible assets, investments, derivative instruments, trade receivables, loans, cash, and other financial assets. It also lists equity and liabilities: equity attributable to owners and non-controlling interests, non-current liabilities (borrowings, lease liabilities, provisions, deferred tax), and current liabilities (borrowings, trade payables, provisions, tax liabilities). Total assets, liabilities, and equity are provided. The document includes notes 1 to 44, auditor’s report reference, and signatories (Chairman, Vice Chairman & MD, CFO, Company Secretary, and auditor) with date May 13, 2025, New Delhi.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss
nodes.summary: The text presents Bharti Airtel Limited's Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended March 31, 2025, including the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss, Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity, and Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows. It details income, expenses, profit before tax, tax expenses, profit for the year, other comprehensive income, total comprehensive income, earnings per share, and equity movements. The cash flow statement covers operating, investing, and financing activities, with comparatives for March 31, 2024. It also includes board and auditor signatures, notes, and references to accompanying notes.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: The section presents Bharti Airtel's Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows for 2025 and 2024, covering operating, investing, and financing activities, and includes extensive notes on accounting policies: consolidation, subsidiaries, joint ventures, associates, business combinations, foreign currency, hyperinflation, financial instruments, derivatives, hedging, derecognition, leases, income taxes, employee benefits, provisions, revenue recognition, dividends, government grants, borrowing costs, exceptional items, and earnings per share. It also covers estimation uncertainties, critical judgements, significant transactions (FCCBs, Indus Towers, spectrum, divestments, IPOs, buybacks), impairment reviews for Airtel Africa and other operations, investments in joint ventures and associates, contingent liabilities (tax, customs, entry tax, stamp duty, entertainment tax, DoT demands), capital commitments, revenue disaggregation, contract balances, expenses, exceptional items, segment reporting, and related party disclosures.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents Bharti Airtel Limited's Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows for the years ended March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, detailing cash flows from operating, investing, and financing activities, including adjustments for non-cash items, changes in assets and liabilities, and specific transactions such as spectrum payments and borrowings. It also includes notes to the consolidated financial statements, covering corporate information, basis of preparation, new amendments adopted, basis of measurement, fair value measurement, and basis of consolidation, with references to accompanying notes and board approvals.

nodes.title: a. Subsidiaries
nodes.summary: The text covers consolidation principles: subsidiaries (control definition, consolidation dates, NCI treatment, put options, disposal accounting), joint ventures and associates (definitions, equity method, impairment), and method of consolidation (policy alignment, line-by-line consolidation, eliminations, equity method mechanics). It details business combinations using the acquisition method (fair value measurement, NCI, contingent consideration, goodwill, acquisition costs, provisional accounting, contingent liabilities). Foreign currency transactions are addressed: functional currency, translation of transactions and balances, foreign operations translation with FCTR, and net investment in foreign operations. Finally, hyperinflation accounting for Malawi under Ind AS 29 is explained, including revaluation and comparative treatment.

nodes.title: Joint Ventures, Associates, Consolidation, Business Combinations, and Foreign Currency
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting for joint ventures and associates using the equity method, including impairment testing. It details the consolidation method: aligning accounting policies, full line-by-line consolidation of subsidiaries, elimination of intra-group transactions and unrealized gains/losses, and equity method accounting for joint ventures and associates with goodwill recognition, loss limitation, and impairment assessment. It also covers business combinations using the acquisition method, including fair value measurement, non-controlling interests, contingent consideration, goodwill, acquisition costs, provisional accounting, and contingent liabilities. Finally, it addresses foreign currency transactions, including functional and presentation currency, translation of transactions and balances, and translation of foreign operations with exchange differences recognized in OCI and reclassified on disposal.

nodes.title: d. Net Investment in Foreign Operations
key_items: I. Initial measurement; II. Subsequent measurement - financial assets
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies under Ind AS: net investment in foreign operations and FCTR reclassification on disposal; hyperinflation accounting for Malawi under Ind AS 29, including CPI use, revaluation of non-monetary items, gain/loss on net monetary assets, and hyperinflation adjustment reserve; current/non-current classification criteria; PPE recognition, cost components, subsequent measurement, depreciation methods and useful lives, reviews, and derecognition; intangible assets including goodwill, finite-lived intangibles, software and spectrum amortization, and IAUD; impairment of goodwill and other non-financial assets, including reversal rules; financial instruments recognition, classification, initial and subsequent measurement (amortized cost, FVTOCI, FVTPL), expected credit losses, derivative measurement, hedging including net investment hedge, and derecognition; leases for lessee and lessor including ROU, lease liabilities, short-term/low-value exemptions, finance and operating leases, and IRU arrangements; and income taxes covering current tax, uncertain tax treatments, and offsetting.

nodes.title: Measurement of Derivatives and Hedging Activities
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting for compound financial instruments, derivative financial instruments, and hedging activities. It explains that the liability component of compound instruments is measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method, while the equity component is not re-measured; interest is recognized in profit or loss, and upon conversion or maturity, the liability is reclassified to equity with no gain or loss. Derivatives not designated as hedging instruments are classified as FVTPL held for trading, initially at fair value with subsequent changes in profit or loss. For net investment hedges, effective portions of foreign exchange differences are recognized in OCI as FCTR, ineffective portions in profit or loss, and accumulated amounts are reclassified to profit or loss upon disposal of the foreign operation.

nodes.title: e. Derecognition
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: derecognition of financial assets and liabilities; leases (lessee and lessor accounting, ROU assets, lease liabilities, short-term/low-value leases, finance/operating leases, IRU arrangements); income taxes (current and deferred tax, MAT, uncertain tax positions); inventories; cash and cash equivalents; share capital and treasury shares; employee benefits (defined contribution/benefit plans, compensated absences, share-based payments); provisions (general and asset retirement obligations); contingencies; and revenue recognition (service revenues, multiple-element arrangements, equipment sales, interest income, and costs to obtain or fulfil contracts).

nodes.title: f. Dividend income
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for dividend income, government grants (income and PPE-related), borrowing costs (capitalization of qualifying assets), exceptional items, dividends paid, and earnings per share (basic and diluted). It also discusses key sources of estimation uncertainties (impairment reviews, taxes, PPE useful lives, trade receivables impairment, contingent liabilities) and critical judgements in applying accounting policies (revenue recognition, lease component separation, lease term determination, incremental borrowing rate, functional currency, and deferred taxes).

nodes.title: g. Hyperinflation
nodes.summary: The text covers hyperinflation accounting for Malawi operations, detailing the criteria for determining hyperinflation and the resulting adjustments to financial statements. It then describes significant transactions: conversion and redemption of FCCBs, acquisition of control in Indus Towers with provisional goodwill and gain on fair valuation, prepayment of spectrum liabilities, dilution of investment in OneWeb, disposal of Airtel Lanka for a stake in Dialog Axiata, participation in spectrum auction, tax and regulatory updates from Supreme Court judgments, foreign exchange gains/losses from currency devaluations in Nigeria, Tanzania, and Malawi, share buy-back programs by Airtel Africa, acquisition of additional stake in Airtel Africa, redemption of perpetual bonds, IPO of Bharti Hexacom, acquisition of Beetel Teletech, IPO of Airtel Uganda, and dilution of stake in Airtel Payments Bank due to rights issue. It also includes a reconciliation of PPE and CWIP, goodwill and intangible assets, and impairment review of goodwill.

nodes.title: A. Impairment review of goodwill pertaining to Airtel Africa operations
nodes.summary: The text details the impairment review of goodwill for Airtel Africa's operations as of December 31, 2024. It lists carrying values for Nigeria Mobile Services, East Africa Mobile Services, Francophone Africa Mobile Services, and Mobile Money Services. Recoverable amounts are based on value-in-use using ten-year business plans approved by the Board, justified by underpenetrated markets, ten-year license/asset lives, and growth opportunities. Sensitivity analysis using a five-year plan showed no impairment and less than 4% decrease in recoverable value. Climate change impact is considered and no impairment resulted. Key assumptions include pre-tax discount rates, capital expenditure, and long-term growth rates. Impairment testing concluded no impairment, with recoverable amounts exceeding carrying amounts by significant margins. Breakeven discount rates and sensitivity analysis are provided. The prior year (2023) impairment assessment is also summarized, showing no impairment and similar assumptions and results.

nodes.title: B. Impairment review of goodwill pertaining to operations other than Airtel Africa
nodes.summary: The text covers impairment review of goodwill for operations excluding Airtel Africa, detailing the use of ten-year business plans for value-in-use calculations due to growing markets and spectrum life, key assumptions (EBITDA margins, discount rates, growth rates, capex), sensitivity assessment, and no impairment in December 2024. It also discusses goodwill allocated to Passive Infrastructure CGU (Indus Towers) not tested due to recent acquisition. Additionally, it presents investments in joint ventures and associates with balance sheet and profit/loss amounts, summarized financial information for material joint ventures (Indus Towers, Robi Axiata, Airtel Payments Bank) and associates, details of joint ventures and associates, investments in subsidiaries with summarized financial information for material NCI (Nxtra, Bharti Hexacom, Indus Towers, Airtel Africa), investments, derivative financial instruments, other financial assets, income tax (expense, reconciliation, deferred tax), other assets, trade receivables, cash and bank balances, share capital, other equity, borrowings, other financial liabilities, provisions, other liabilities, trade payables, and contingencies and commitments.

nodes.title: Contingent Liabilities: Tax, Customs, Entry Tax, and Municipal Stamp Duty Disputes
nodes.summary: This page presents Bharti Airtel's notes on contingencies and commitments, detailing contingent liabilities as of March 31, 2025 and 2024. It lists claims not acknowledged as debt across taxes, duties, and legal cases, including sales tax, service tax, GST, income tax, customs duty, entry tax, municipal tax, stamp duty, DoT demands, entertainment tax, and miscellaneous demands. It also includes the Group's share of joint ventures' and associates' contingent liabilities. Category-wise details cover sales tax/VAT, service tax, income tax appeals, customs duty issues (export obligations, classification, FTA benefits, valuation, anti-dumping), entry tax constitutional challenges and GST input tax credit disallowances, and municipal tax/stamp duty on cell site agreements.

nodes.title: f) Entertainment tax
nodes.summary: The entertainment tax section covers contingent liabilities for entertainment tax on subscription and activation charges, Department of Telecommunications regulatory demands (disputed enhanced microwave rates, Unified License migration, license fees on internet service revenue, subscriber verification norms, EMF radiation penalties, additional spectrum usage charges), one-time spectrum charge litigation, 3G intra-circle roaming penalties, and a tax offset agreement from the Airtel Bangladesh-Robi Axiata merger. It also includes capital commitments, revenue disaggregation by geography, service line, and timing, contract balances, costs to obtain contracts, other income, network operating expenses, employee benefits (retirement and compensated absence plans with actuarial assumptions and sensitivity analysis), share-based payment plans, sales and marketing expenses, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses, finance costs, exceptional items for 2025 and 2024 (gains/losses from business combinations, regulatory levies, impairments, forex, divestments, tax matters), earnings per share calculations, segment reporting, and related party disclosures.

nodes.title: f) Entertainment tax (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers contingent liabilities for entertainment tax on subscription and activation charges, and Department of Telecommunications (DoT) regulatory demands, including disputes over enhanced microwave rates, Unified License migration and license fees on internet service revenue, subscriber verification norms, EMF radiation penalties, and additional spectrum usage charges. It details one-time spectrum charge (OTSC) litigation, 3G intra-circle roaming penalties, and a tax offset agreement from the Airtel Bangladesh-Robi Axiata merger. Capital commitments are disclosed. Revenue from operations is disaggregated by geographical market, service line, and timing, with contract balances, costs to obtain contracts, other income, network operating expenses, employee benefits, and share-based payment plans outlined.

nodes.title: Plan
nodes.summary: This section presents notes to Bharti Airtel's consolidated financial statements, covering contract balances, costs to obtain or fulfil contracts, other income, network operating expenses, employee benefits (including retirement and compensated absence plans with actuarial assumptions and sensitivity analysis), share-based payment plans with detailed option movements and fair value inputs. It details sales and marketing expenses, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses, finance costs, and exceptional items for 2025 and 2024, including gains/losses from business combinations, regulatory levies, impairments, forex, divestments, and tax matters. It also covers earnings per share calculations with reconciliation of weighted average shares, segment reporting by business segments with revenue, results, assets, liabilities, and capital expenditure, and related party disclosures listing entities and key management personnel.

nodes.title: Plan (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents notes to Bharti Airtel's consolidated financial statements, covering contract balances (unbilled revenue, deferred revenue, and reconciliations), costs to obtain or fulfil contracts, other income details, network operating expenses, employee benefits expense, and share-based payment plans. It includes tables for contract balances, cost reconciliation, other income, network expenses, employee benefits, and share option plans with vesting periods and contractual terms. Detailed movements in stock options for various plans (LTI, Nxtra, IPO, performance, restricted, etc.) are provided, along with fair value measurement inputs using the Black-Scholes model and weighted average remaining contractual life, fair value, and share price for options.

nodes.title: 27.2 Employee benefits
nodes.summary: The text details employee benefits, specifically retirement and compensated absence plans, for the years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024. It presents the present value of obligations, plan assets, net liability, and expected contributions. It includes amounts recognized in OCI, notes that plan assets are invested with LIC, and outlines risks such as changes in bond yields and salary risk. Actuarial assumptions (discount rate, salary increase, attrition, retirement age) are provided, along with sensitivity analysis of the defined benefit obligation to changes in discount rate and salary growth. A maturity profile and weighted average duration of the gratuity liability are also summarized.

nodes.title: 28Sales and marketing expenses
nodes.summary: The text presents notes to Bharti Airtel's consolidated financial statements for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024. It details expenses: sales and marketing (commissions, advertising, promotion, ancillary); depreciation and amortisation (PPE, ROU, intangibles); other expenses (content, cost of sales, IT, customer care, legal, doubtful receivables, collection, travel, bad debts, charity, others including political contributions); finance costs (interest, lease liabilities, forex loss, derivatives, other charges). Exceptional items for both years include gains/losses from Indus business combination, regulatory levies, impairments, forex, divestments, tax matters, and legal settlements.
